ai.literal: To those who are poor, giving something is indeed true charity; all other giving possesses the nature of expecting a return gift.
ai.translation: Giving to the poor is true charity; all other giving is of the nature of a loan expecting a return.
ai.modern: வறியவர்களுக்கு ஏதேனும் ஒன்றைக் கொடுப்பதே ஈகை ஆகும்; மற்றபடி பிறருக்குக் கொடுப்பதெல்லாம் திரும்பப் பெறும் நோக்கம் உடைய கடனைப் போன்ற தன்மையைக் கொண்டது.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true essence of charity. Giving to those who are completely destitute and have nothing is the only real act of giving. Any other form of giving, such as giving to friends, relatives, or those who can repay, is not true charity. Instead, it is like a transaction or a loan given with the expectation of a future return or benefit.

ai.literal: Even if it is said to be a good path, receiving is bad; even if it is said that the upper world does not exist, giving indeed is good.
ai.translation: Even if receiving gifts is said to be a path to goodness, it is bad. Even if there is no higher world to be gained, giving to others is still the best path.
ai.modern: பிறரிடமிருந்து பொருளைப் பெறுவது நல்ல வழி என்று சொன்னாலும் அது தீமையானது; கொடையளிப்பதால் மேலுலகம் கிடைக்காது என்றாலும் பிறருக்குக் கொடுப்பதே நல்லது.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the acts of receiving and giving to establish the supreme value of charity. The author states that accepting things from others is inherently degrading and bad, even if someone claims it is a righteous path. On the other hand, giving to those in need is inherently noble and good, even if there is no heavenly reward or higher world awaiting the giver. Virtue in giving lies in the act itself, not in the expectation of spiritual or material returns.

ai.literal: Giving without letting the destitute speak the distress of saying 'I have nothing' exists only with one who has noble lineage.
ai.translation: Giving to the needy even before they have to utter the painful words, 'I have nothing,' is a virtue found only in those of noble birth.
ai.modern: 'எனக்கு ஒன்றும் இல்லை' என்று இரப்பவர் தன் துன்பத்தைச் சொல்லும் முன்பே அவருக்குக் கொடுக்கும் குணம், நற்குடியில் பிறந்தவரிடமே இருக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the highest form of charity. True giving does not wait for a needy person to undergo the painful humiliation of begging and uttering the words 'I have nothing' (இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம்). A person of noble character and lineage (குலனுடையான்) senses the distress of others and gives generously before they even have to ask (உரையாமை ஈதல்). This proactive generosity is described as a rare quality that exists only with those of noble birth.

ai.literal: Being begged of is painful, until the moment of seeing the pleasant face of those who begged.
ai.translation: Being begged for alms is painful, but only until one sees the joyful, pleasant face of those who receive the gift.
ai.modern: பிறர் நம்மிடம் வந்து இரந்து கேட்பது துன்பமானதுதான்; ஆனால், இரந்து கேட்டவரின் மகிழ்ச்சியான முகத்தைக் காணும் வரை மட்டுமே அத்துன்பம் நீடிக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explores the psychological experience of giving charity. The act of being asked for help (irakka-patutal) can initially feel unpleasant or painful (innatu) to a giver, perhaps due to the burden of giving or witnessing another's distress. However, this discomfort lasts only until (alavu) the giver beholds the sweet, joyful face (inmukam) of the recipient upon receiving the aid. The sight of the beggar's happiness instantly transforms the giver's pain into profound joy, highlighting the ultimate reward of charity.

ai.literal: The power of those who perform penance is enduring hunger; (but) that is behind the power of those who remove that hunger.
ai.translation: The power of those who perform penance lies in enduring their own hunger; yet, that power is only secondary to the power of those who alleviate the hunger of others.
ai.modern: தவம் செய்வோரின் வலிமை என்பது பசியைப் பொறுத்துக் கொள்வதாகும்; ஆனால், அந்த வலிமையானது பிறருடைய பசியைப் போக்குபவர்களின் வலிமைக்கு அடுத்ததாகவே மதிக்கப்படும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares two kinds of strength: the strength of ascetics who perform penance by enduring hunger, and the strength of givers who remove the hunger of others. The author states that while enduring hunger is a great feat of self-control, it is subordinate to the noble act of giving food to satisfy another's hunger. The word 'ஆற்றல்' is used in two senses: first as 'power' or 'strength' and second as 'enduring' (from the verb 'ஆற்று'). The word 'பின்' (behind or after) establishes a clear hierarchy, placing the altruistic act of giving above the self-focused act of ascetic endurance.

ai.literal: Relieving the ruinous hunger of the destitute, that is the place where a man who has obtained wealth stores it.
ai.translation: Relieving the ruinous hunger of the destitute is the very place where a man who has acquired wealth should store it.
ai.modern: வறியவர்களின் அழிக்கும் பசியைத் தீர்ப்பதுதான், செல்வம் பெற்ற ஒருவன் தன் பொருளைச் சேமித்து வைக்கும் இடமாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the true and secure way to store one's wealth. It states that satisfying the intense, ruinous hunger of the destitute is the ultimate treasury for a wealthy person. Rather than hoarding riches in physical vaults where they can be lost, spending them to feed the needy acts as an imperishable storehouse. The word 'அழிபசி' highlights the devastating nature of hunger, while 'வைப்புழி' metaphorically frames charity as the safest place of deposit.

ai.literal: Sharing food, having accustomed himself to it, him, hunger called fiery-disease, touching, is rare.
ai.translation: The fiery disease of hunger will never touch the one who has made a habit of sharing his food with others.
ai.modern: தன் உணவைப் பிறரோடு பகிர்ந்து உண்ணும் பழக்கத்தைக் கொண்டவனை, பசி என்று சொல்லப்படும் கொடிய நோய் தீண்டுவது இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the protective power of charity. The poet compares hunger to a 'fiery disease' (தீப்பிணி) because of the intense, burning pain and suffering it inflicts on the body. The word 'மரீஇ' indicates a deep-seated habit or custom; it is not about a one-time act of giving, but rather about someone who has integrated sharing into their daily life. The couplet assures us that such a generous person will never suffer from the misery of hunger, as their virtue and the goodwill of those they helped will always sustain them.

ai.literal: Having given, the rejoicing pleasure, do they not know indeed? Their own wealth, having stored, losing, the hard-hearted people.
ai.translation: Do those hard-hearted people, who hoard their wealth only to lose it eventually, not know the joy that comes from giving?
ai.modern: பிறருக்குக் கொடுத்து மகிழும் இன்பத்தை அறிய மாட்டார்களோ? தம்மிடமுள்ள செல்வத்தைச் சேர்த்து வைத்துப் பின் அதனை இழந்துவிடும் இரக்கமற்றவர்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the joy of charity with the folly of hoarding. The poet refers to those who hoard wealth without sharing it as 'hard-hearted' (vaṉkaṇavar) because they lack the empathy to help others. By keeping their wealth locked away, they inevitably lose it to theft, decay, or death without ever enjoying it. The poet wonders if these people are simply ignorant of the profound happiness (iṉpam) that one experiences when giving to those in need.

ai.literal: Than begging, painful indeed is, having accumulated food, themselves alone in solitude eating.
ai.translation: Eating alone in solitude, having hoarded food only for oneself, is surely more painful than begging for alms.
ai.modern: இரந்து கேட்பதை விட மிகவும் துன்பமானது, தனக்காகச் சேர்த்து வைத்த உணவைத் தான் மட்டும் தனியாக உண்பது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the misery of begging with the selfishness of hoarding. While begging is universally seen as a painful and humiliating state, the poet declares that securing food only for oneself ('nirappiya') and eating it in solitary isolation ('tamiyar uṇal') without sharing is far more wretched. The word 'maṉṟa' acts as an intensifier, emphasizing that this truth is absolute. Thus, the spiritual pain of selfishness is shown to be worse than the physical pain of poverty.

ai.literal: Than dying, a more painful thing there is not; pleasant even that becomes, when giving is not possible.
ai.translation: There is nothing more painful than death; yet even death becomes pleasant when one is unable to give to those in need.
ai.modern: இறப்பதை விடத் துன்பமானது வேறு எதுவும் இல்லை; ஆனால், வறியவர்க்குத் தர முடியாத நிலை ஏற்படும் போது, அந்த இறப்பும் கூட இனியதே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the pain of death with the pain of being unable to practice charity. It begins by stating that nothing is more painful than dying. However, it immediately qualifies this by saying that even death becomes sweet when one's circumstances make giving impossible. The word 'kaṭai' here functions as a conditional marker meaning 'when' or 'in the state of'. Through this stark comparison, the poet emphasizes that for a noble person, the inability to help others is a fate far worse than death itself.
